messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 70
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Welder
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Entrapment: Having no options, Violence: Violence, Auditory/Threat: Gunshot noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Fawn Response: become overly compliant when feeling threatened, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rodrigo is a 70-year-old widowed Latino man who has worked as a welder for most of his adult life, immigrating to the United States from Central America decades ago and building a quiet, self-sufficient existence around his trade. He presented for treatment with a PCL-5 score of 80, describing a level of daily suffering that he had, until recently, tried to manage entirely on his own.

Approximately three years ago, while visiting family in his country of origin, Rodrigo was detained by a group of armed men who accused him of political affiliations he did not hold. He was taken to a location he did not recognize, bound, and subjected to prolonged physical violence over what he believes was two days, though he cannot account for all of the time. At several points during his captivity, a firearm was discharged in close proximity to him — sometimes as a threat, sometimes without apparent reason. He was given no information about whether he would be released or killed, and there were moments when every door, every silence, every shift in his captors' tone felt like it might be the last thing he experienced. He was eventually released without explanation and made his way back across the border. He told no one the full account of what had happened.

In the months that followed, Rodrigo returned to his welding work at a fabrication shop, where the environment — loud, industrial, punctuated by the sharp percussive sounds of pneumatic tools and metal striking metal — became a daily ordeal he navigated without anyone around him understanding why. When a nail gun fired in the adjacent bay or a steel beam dropped unexpectedly, Rodrigo's body responded as though he were still bound in that room. The memory, in those moments, did not feel like something that had ended. It arrived fully, without distance, as though the intervening years had not occurred at all. He found he could not explain this to his supervisor when his work slowed, when he began arriving late to avoid the noisiest parts of the morning shift. He attempted once to describe what had happened to a younger colleague and lost the thread entirely mid-sentence, the account dissolving before he could reach anything coherent, leaving him ashamed and silent.

Rodrigo had come to believe, with a certainty that felt like knowledge rather than fear, that there was no reliable way to identify who might harm him. Strangers, authority figures, even men who reminded him in posture or tone of his captors became objects of quiet, exhaustive vigilance. At the same time, when he sensed any interpersonal tension — a foreman's impatience, a neighbor's irritation — he became accommodating to a degree that felt involuntary, agreeable in ways that afterward left him feeling hollowed out. He worked hard to keep the memories from surfacing, pushing against them deliberately throughout the day, and when they broke through anyway, what rose with them was not grief but rage — a fury so intense it frightened him, directed at the men who had done this and, with equal force, at himself.

What tormented Rodrigo most was not the violence itself but his own conduct during it. He had come to believe that something in the way he had behaved — words he had said, the way he had presented himself in the days before the detention — had made him a target. Worse, he was convinced he had failed to act during his captivity in ways that might have changed the outcome, and he carried this as a permanent verdict on his character. He would never forgive himself for it, he said plainly, as though this were simply a fact.

It was the death of his wife two years prior, and the subsequent absence of the one person to whom he had been even partially known, that finally made the isolation unbearable. His adult children had noticed his withdrawal, his flinching at ordinary sounds, the way he sometimes stopped mid-conversation and seemed to go somewhere else entirely. It was his daughter who made the appointment. Rodrigo came because he was tired — not of living, he was careful to say, but of carrying something this heavy entirely alone. What he hoped for, tentatively, was that some part of it might become possible to set down.
